title: Equality and layout
sub: ValueType.Equals, IEquatable<T>, record struct and the bytes of a struct
cards/0/body:
A struct without its own Equals is compared by value — ValueType.Equals(object) does it. It does not know your fields in advance and goes like this:

  • the argument is null or of another type (checked via GetType) — false;
  • if the struct can be compared byte by byte — it compares the memory of both values as byte arrays. That is fast;
  • otherwise — reflection: it gets the list of fields via GetFields and calls FieldInfo.GetValue on both values for each one. Every value-type field gets boxed along the way, then compared with Equals.

The slow path is several times, even an order of magnitude, slower than a hand-written comparison and allocates on every call.
cards/0/deep: Sources: ValueType.cs in dotnet/runtime (CoreLib) and the CanCompareBitsOrUseFastGetHashCode check in the runtime. The check result is cached in the type data (MethodTable), so the "fast or slow" decision is made once per type.
cards/1/body:
The fast path kicks in only if every condition holds:

  • the struct has no references: two different strings with the same text are different addresses, the bytes will not match;
  • the struct is tightly packed — no alignment gaps. Gaps can hold anything, their bytes are undefined;
  • no float or double fields: 0.0 and -0.0 are equal but have different bytes; NaN is the other way round;
  • neither the struct nor its field types override Equals or GetHashCode.

Break even one — reflection.
cards/1/code:
struct Fast { public int X, Y; }            // bytes
struct Slow1 { public int Id; public string Name; } // a reference
struct Slow2 { public byte Flag; public int Value; } // a 3-byte gap
struct Slow3 { public double X, Y; }        // double
cards/1/deep: The float/double check was not there from the start: in older runtime versions a struct with a double was compared bytewise, and new S(0.0).Equals(new S(-0.0)) returned false even though the fields are equal. Reflection compares fields via double.Equals, for which 0.0 and -0.0 are equal and NaN equals NaN.
cards/2/q: Which structs will ValueType.Equals compare bytewise in modern .NET? None of them overrides anything. Select all.
cards/2/explain: A is 8 bytes with no gaps. E is 8 + 4 + 4 = 16 bytes, aligned with no holes. B has a reference, C has floats, and D has three alignment bytes after the byte before the int: all three go through reflection.
cards/3/title: ValueType.GetHashCode: a hash of one field
cards/3/body:
The default hash also has two paths. The fast one (same conditions) hashes all the bytes of the struct. The slow one hashes only one field: the first one that is not null. The other fields do not go into the hash at all.

Equals still compares every field, so the contract is formally kept. But if the first field is the same for many keys, they all land in one dictionary bucket. Lookup turns from O(1) into walking a chain.
cards/3/deep: The slow path picks the field at run time (GetHashCodeStrategy): a reference — its GetHashCode, double/float — their hash, a nested struct — recursively by the same rules. The struct type is always mixed into the hash. .NET Framework had the same "first field" rule, so the advice "override GetHashCode on a struct key" is not outdated.
cards/4/q: A dictionary holds a million Key { Region, Id } keys, Region is "EU" in all of them. Equals and GetHashCode are not overridden. What happens to lookups?
cards/4/options/0: Every key is in one bucket: each lookup is a long walk with comparisons via reflection
cards/4/options/1: Business as usual: the hash includes Id too
cards/4/options/2: The dictionary throws when a duplicate hash is inserted
cards/4/options/3: Lookups are fast but eat a lot of memory for boxes
cards/4/explain: The slow-path hash comes from the first non-null field — the string "EU". All keys got the same hash, one bucket. Each comparison along the chain is ValueType.Equals via reflection with boxed fields.
cards/4/wrong/2: Equal hashes are an ordinary collision, and Dictionary is ready for it. It just becomes slow.
cards/5/body:
Dictionary, HashSet, List.Contains, Array.IndexOf, Distinct compare through EqualityComparer<T>.Default. It picks an implementation once per type:

  • if T : IEquatable<T> — it calls Equals(T): no boxes, an ordinary method that can be inlined;
  • if not — it calls Equals(object): the argument is boxed, and without an override it goes on to ValueType.Equals.

The full set for a struct: IEquatable<T>, an Equals(object) that calls it, GetHashCode over the same fields, and the ==/!= operators.
cards/5/deep: For a value-type T the JIT knows the exact type of EqualityComparer<T>.Default and since .NET Core 2.1 devirtualizes the call: Dictionary<int, …> compares keys almost like hand-written code. That is why Dictionary even has a separate code branch for value-type keys without a custom comparer.
cards/6/q: Complete equality with no boxes and no reflection
cards/6/explain: IEquatable<Point> gives collections Equals(Point) without boxing. Equals(object) just delegates to it so the two methods never diverge. ReferenceEquals is always false for a struct: two boxes are two objects.
cards/7/title: record struct writes it for you
cards/7/body:
Since C# 10 a record struct generates everything from the previous card: IEquatable<T>, Equals(T) over all fields via EqualityComparer<TField>.Default, Equals(object), GetHashCode, ==, != and a ToString that shows the contents. No reflection, no boxes.

The difference from a plain struct shows at once: a plain struct has no == operator, and a == b does not compile (CS0019). The compiler does not try to guess what value equality means.

Remember: the positional properties of a record struct are mutable (get; set;). The immutable flavor is readonly record struct.
cards/7/deep: The generated equality compares double fields via double.Equals, not via ==. So two records with a double.NaN field are equal (a == b is True), even though NaN == NaN is false. This is by design: otherwise such a record could never be found in a dictionary.
cards/8/q: P is a plain struct with fields X and Y and no operators. What happens?
cards/8/explain: A struct has no == operator until you write one (or declare a record struct). Equals is always there — ValueType provides it — but the operator is not.
cards/8/wrong/2: False for two different objects is what == on a class would give — it compares references. A struct simply has no ==.
cards/9/body:
For structs the C# compiler emits [StructLayout(LayoutKind.Sequential)]: fields go in declaration order. But each field is aligned to its size: a long to an address that is a multiple of 8, an int to 4. And the size of the whole struct is rounded up to the strictest alignment, so that every element in an array is aligned too.

Field order changes the size. To find it out without unsafe — Unsafe.SizeOf<T>().
cards/9/code:
struct Loose { byte A; long B; byte C; }   // 1 + 7 gap + 8 + 1 + 7 gap
struct Tight { long B; byte A; byte C; }   // 8 + 1 + 1 + 6 gap

Unsafe.SizeOf<Loose>();   // 24
Unsafe.SizeOf<Tight>();   // 16
cards/9/deep: The numbers are for x64. An empty struct takes 1 byte: every value must have its own address. sizeof(T) for your own structs requires an unsafe context in C#, Unsafe.SizeOf<T> does not — it is a JIT intrinsic.
cards/10/q: Arrange the struct fields so that Sequential layout leaves no gaps between them: from largest to smallest
cards/10/explain: 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15 bytes of data, each field already at an aligned address. The size rounds up to 16 — one gap at the end. Largest to smallest is a simple way not to lose bytes.
cards/11/body:
• LayoutKind.Auto — the runtime reorders fields itself, usually more tightly. But such a struct cannot be passed to unmanaged code.
  • Pack = 1 — no alignment: Loose becomes 10 bytes, but reading an unaligned long may cost more.
  • LayoutKind.Explicit + [FieldOffset] — a field at an exact offset, fields may overlap.

An important caveat from the docs: if a struct has references, Sequential does not control its layout in managed memory — the runtime lays such fields out as Auto. Sequential then only affects marshaling.

And the link back to the start of the lesson: alignment gaps disable the bytewise ValueType.Equals.
cards/11/deep:
Marshal.SizeOf<T>() is the size when marshaled, not in .NET memory. For struct { bool A; bool B; } Unsafe.SizeOf is 2, while Marshal.SizeOf is 8: by default bool is marshaled as a 4-byte Win32 BOOL.

The "version 2" scenario: reorder the fields of a Sequential struct that goes to P/Invoke or is written to a file as bytes, and native code and old files now read the wrong fields. For such structs the field order is part of the contract.
cards/12/q: Match each tool with what it gives you
cards/12/pairs/1/1: The size when passed to unmanaged code
cards/12/pairs/2/1: The runtime picks the field order
cards/12/pairs/3/1: Fields back to back with no alignment
cards/12/pairs/4/1: A field at an exact offset
